For a frozen model and deterministically selected users, define the estimand explicitly: the selected-user average expected diagnostic under a specified random intervention distribution, conditional on the fitted checkpoint and observed histories. Resample whole users, retaining all five permutations and intervention conditions together; for category-macro summaries, resample users within each category and preserve equal category weighting. Such bootstrap intervals describe sensitivity to reweighting the selected users, under an empirical user-distribution interpretation. They do not establish population coverage or generalization to unseen users; deterministic selection supplies no probability-sampling justification. This distinction follows the sampling-versus-design framework in [Abadie et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.02926).

Separate finite Monte Carlo error from user heterogeneity. For independent permutations, let s_u² be the within-user sample variance across five draws. For an equally weighted mean over U fixed users, estimated MCSE = sqrt[sum_u s_u²/(5U²)], assuming independent draws across users. With general weights w_u, use sqrt[sum_u w_u² s_u²/5]. Five draws give noisy variance estimates; report the draw count, seed, and MCSE without implying precise tail coverage. [Morris, White and Crowther](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6492164/) emphasize reporting uncertainty caused by finite simulation repetitions.

Compare intervention distributions through within-user contrasts. If draws use a valid shared-randomness coupling, calculate each paired difference and estimate MCSE from its variance, retaining covariance; otherwise, add the independently estimated Monte Carlo variances. Bootstrap the same user indices across conditions. Pairing by user does not itself pair independent permutation draws. These are conditional diagnostic contrasts, not causal effects or uncertainty over retraining; the formulas above apply standard Monte Carlo variance propagation to this diagnostic design.
